## 1. Caston 2021 — *Aristotle on the Cartesian Theatre*

**Bibliographic anchor**: Caston, V. (2021), "Aristotle on the Cartesian Theatre," in Caleb Cohoe (ed.), *Aristotle's De Anima: A Critical Guide* (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press), ch. 7.

**ChromaDB filter**: `dissertation-perplexity-cache`, `{"author": "Caston, Victor"}` → 29 chunks.

**Key concept-cluster**: phantasia content-theory; phantasma as "both something in itself and a phantasma of something else"; controlling sense (τὸ κύριον καὶ τὸ ἐπικρῖνον) vs. imaging faculty; non-identity of faculties; copy/reminder structure; lucid-dream and Coriscus passages.

**Top-relevance chunks (by minimum cosine distance across 5 queries)**:

### Chunk 11 (book pp.~188-189) — dist 0.4380, query: non-identity-faculties

> "The difference, Aristotle suggests, is to be explained by the fact that in the first case, rather than just taking a visualization on its own, I also regard it as a copy of a past experience. Perceiving it this way is not so much a matter of scrutinizing a picture, but a form of recognition: it is a matter of regarding it in a certain way, of seeing it as familiar, as something I have gone through before. [...] This reading is confirmed by Aristotle's description of cases where we doubt that we are remembering: although the relevant changes in fact arise 'from an earlier perceiving' (ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰσθέσθαι), we vacillate [...]"

**Relevance for dissertation**: Direct phenomenology of remembering-vs-imagining as it relates to phantasma-recognition. Useful for §1.3 (A3 memory subsection) and §1.4 (resonant-pathē-via-memory-phantasma).

### Chunk 23 (book pp.~212-213) — dist 0.4445, query: controlling-sense-judgement

> "[Aristotle] differentiates two senses of being 'like' (ὅμοιον): in the second sense, one thing is not only like another, but 'has the same form from that thing' (ὡς ἀπ' ἐκείνου τὸ ταὐτὸν εἶδος ἔχον, 912.37). [...] But the only difference with artistic copies is that Platonic forms are both the model and what produces the copy, something that would be true for Aristotle as well in the natural generation [...]"

**Relevance**: Caston's structural reading of phantasma-as-copy (εἰκὼν) versus phantasma-in-itself, with explicit cross-reference to *Memory* 452b26-29. Foundational for the dissertation's `resonant aisthēma` apparatus.

### Chunk 7 (book pp.~180-181) — dist 0.4520, query: phantasia-content-theory [LOAD-BEARING for DISS-04-C190]

> "[...] one must conceive of the phantasma in us, which is both something in itself and a phantasma of something else [ἄλλου]: insofar as it is something in itself, it is something considered or a phantasma, while insofar as it is of something else [ᾗ δ' ἄλλου] it is like a copy [οἷον εἰκὼν], that is, a reminder."

**Relevance**: THE canonical 21st-century gloss on phantasma's dual mode. Already cited in DISS-04-G-C190-tier-b.md citation fill.

### Chunk 13 (book pp.~192-193) — dist 0.4783, query: controlling-sense-judgement [LOAD-BEARING for DISS-04-C190]

> "Sometimes we are aware that we are asleep, a higher-order awareness he again expresses with 'perceives' (αἰσθάνεσθαι), and so have what we would call a 'lucid dream' (462a2–8)" — citing Aristotle: "ᾧ δὴ καὶ αἰσθανόμενον λέγει τοῦτο, ἐὰν μὴ παντελῶς κατέχηται ὑπὸ τοῦ αἵματος [...] φαίνεται μέν, λέγει δέ τι ἐν αὐτῷ ὅτι φαίνεται μὲν Κορίσκος, οὐκ ἔστι δὲ ὁ Κορίσκος (πολλάκις γὰρ καθεύδοντος λέγει τι ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ὅτι ἐνύπνιον τὸ φαινόμενον)·"

**Relevance**: The Coriscus / "controlling and adjudicating" (τὸ κύριον καὶ τὸ ἐπικρῖνον) passage at *On Dreams* 462a2-8 — direct anchor for the non-identity-of-faculties thesis. Already cited in DISS-04-G-C190-tier-b.md.

### Chunk 15 (book pp.~196-197) — dist 0.4663, query: non-identity-faculties

> "The perceptual stimulation, in turn, produces a phantasma, which, as we have seen, is 'like a kind of impression' (οἷον τύπον τινά) of the stimulation (Mem. 1, 450a31), which can be stored and later reactivated. Because of the way they are produced, the latter is a similar change to the original perceptual stimulation, and in Aristotle's view therefore gives rise to an experience with a similar content."

**Relevance**: Caston's structural account of why phantasmata produced by past perceptual stimulation can carry sense-perceptual content — the operative mechanism for `resonant aisthēma` and `resonant epithymia`.

### Chunk 12 (book pp.~190-191) — dist 0.4691, query: controlling-sense-judgement

> "Statements in our soul (τῶν λεγομένων εἰκόνας ἐν τῆ ψυχῇ τούτων γράφει, 39b6-7; τὰς τῶν δοξασθέντων καὶ λεχθέντων εἰκόνας, b10-c1, d7), at least for perceptual beliefs (b8-c1). In such cases, Socrates says, the subject in some way sees these copies 'within himself' (ἐν αὑτῷ ὁρᾷ πως, c1). With our hopes too, we can visualize wished for scenarios [...]"

**Relevance**: The Theaetetus / Plato anchor for "painted phantasmata" — useful for §1.4 doxa-as-cognitive-gate and §1.3 A3 phantasma-articulation.

### Chunk 10 (book pp.~186-187) — dist 0.4649

> "The exhaustiveness of this division confirms that Aristotle's purpose in introducing the distinction between regarding a phantasma as a copy and in itself is a narrow one, which he introduces in order to explain the differences between various states having to do with memory."

**Relevance**: Caston explicitly defends a memory-grounded reading of the phantasma-as-copy / phantasma-in-itself distinction. Useful for the dissertation's claim that memory-phantasmata elicit `resonant pathē`.

### Chunk 18 (book pp.~202-203) — dist 0.4857

> "Note in particular Osborne's statement that phantasia, while it has 'presentational' activities, does not [...] present an alternative inner set of objects to perception or thought, as though one watched an internal slide show of fantastic images [...] We remain observers of the forms directly encountered in perception, not observers of our inner cognitive experiences"

**Relevance**: Caston engages the major debate on whether phantasmata are "inner objects" — recommends a non-Cartesian, content-theoretic reading. This is the entire thesis of his "Cartesian Theatre" critique.

**Downstream value**: Caston 2021 is HIGH PRIORITY for a future corpus/index pipeline. The 29 ingested chunks contain ~10 dissertation-load-bearing passages spanning §1.3 (A3 memory), §1.4 (doxa-gate, faculty-non-identity), and supporting material for the `resonant aisthēma` / `resonant epithymia` analytical apparatus.

## 2. Agosta 2010 — *Heidegger's 1924 Clearing of the Affects Using Aristotle's Rhetoric Book II*

**Bibliographic anchor**: Agosta, Lou (2010), "Heidegger's 1924 Clearing of the Affects Using Aristotle's Rhetoric, Book II," *Philosophy Today* 54(4): 333–345.

**ChromaDB filter**: `dissertation-perplexity-cache`, `{"author": "Agosta, Lou"}` → 17 chunks.

**Key concept-cluster**: Befindlichkeit, Stimmung, clearing, pathē as Dasein's self-disclosure, BCAP/GA 18, fear as mode of affectivity, four-mode pathē taxonomy (hard-coded, social pretense, eruptive, mood).

**Top-relevance chunks**:

### Chunk 5 (p.~335) — dist 0.3708, query: emotion-attunement-world

> "Aristotle discusses the pathē as those phenomena in which it is shown that the concrete being of human beings can only be understood if one takes it in its fullness. [...] It is, above all, decisive that we lose our composure, as in the case of fearing without encountering something in the environing world that could be the direct occasion of fear. (1924: 139–40)" — Agosta then comments: "In particular, the example in the last sentence points to the understanding of affects as disclosive of a whole way of being-in-the-world, not just particular things. [...] All roads—and fears—lead to Dasein; and Dasein is inevitably the about which (woran) of fear."

**Relevance**: LOAD-BEARING for §1.4 (DISS-04-EMOTION). Affects as disclosive of being-in-the-world, not just particular intentional objects. Anchors BCAP-133/Befindlichkeit doctrine in the dissertation.

### Chunk 13 (p.~342) — dist 0.4404, query: emotion-attunement-world

> "[...] Aristotle's pathē are an ad hoc grouping, albeit based on Aristotle's customary comprehension and rigor, and assembled together for the benefit of training the speaker in rhetoric, one should be also able to find examples of all of the distinctions that fall into each of the diverging categories — hard-coded response, social pretense, irruptive reaction, and mood. [...] How this maps to Heidegger's distinction of Befindlichkeit is indicated at the level of the text above (§30 of Being and Time, 'Fear as a Mode of Affectivity' [H 140–42]) as the way the world is disclosed to Dasein."

**Relevance**: Agosta's four-mode taxonomy (hard-coded / social pretense / irruptive / mood) maps onto the dissertation's distinction between live *epithymia* (hard-coded basic-valence), `resonant epithymia` (residual-tonal mood), and articulationally-concrete *pathē* (anger, fear, etc.). USEFUL for §1.4 Feedback Loop subsection.

### Chunk 4 (pp.~334-335) — dist 0.4499, query: aristotle-rhetoric-book-ii

> "For Heidegger, the analysis at the level of Aristotle's Rhetoric requires that the pathē have [...]"

**Relevance**: Short fragment but locates Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's pathē at the level of GA 18 (1924 lecture course) — useful citation anchor.

### Chunk 8 (pp.~337-338) — dist 0.5093

> "Examples where true belief or knowledge does not make a difference to one's affects are common. Darwin knew the cobra was safely locked away [...]" + "Pathē are candidate instances of 'social pretences' built around roles in human relations at the level of the inauthentic das Man"

**Relevance**: Agosta's four-mode taxonomy plus the cognitive-impenetrability case (Darwin / cobra). Useful for §1.4 doxa-as-cognitive-gate when arguing for the irreducibility of certain pathē to doxa alone (i.e., the hard-coded layer).

**Relevance**: Agosta's "hard-coded somatic patterns" maps onto the dissertation's basic-valence stratum (*epithymia* live + `resonant epithymia` residual). The Heideggerian-thrownness / Aristotelian-hyle pair is a model the dissertation can cite directly.

## 3. Dow 2011 — *Aristotle's Theory of the Emotions: Emotions as Pleasures*

**Bibliographic anchor**: Dow, Jamie (2011), *Aristotle's Theory of the Emotions: Emotions as Pleasures* (PhD thesis / monograph; 272 pp).

**ChromaDB filter**: `dissertation-perplexity-cache`, `{"author": "Dow, Jamie"}` → 228 chunks.

**Key concept-cluster**: emotions as pleasures/pains; doxa/belief as necessary condition for emotion; phantasia vs belief in emotion; rhetoric and emotion-arousal; emulation/envy/anger/fear catalog; sun-example argument.

**Top-relevance chunks**:

### Chunk 208 (pp.~251-252) — dist 0.3398, query: epithymia-orexis-pathē [LOAD-BEARING for §1.4]

> "The contrast here is between belief and phantasia, as the context makes clear, in relation to a similar object. Aristotle's point is that belief is sufficient for emotion, whereas phantasia is not. Taken together, this strongly suggests (though it is not explicit) that Aristotle's position is that belief is also necessary for emotion. If that were correct, then Aristotle's position here is entirely consistent with the position we set out earlier from the Rhetoric, that it is essential to emotions that they involve taking things to be a certain way, i.e. that 'beliefs' are essential to emotions. [...] Aristotle's assertion about fear in this passage is very close to what he says in Rhetoric II.5, 1382b33, 'those who believe they might suffer something necessarily are afraid.'"

**Relevance**: LOAD-BEARING for the doxa-gate thesis in §1.4. Dow argues that doxa is BOTH sufficient AND necessary for emotion. The dissertation's doxa-cognitive-gate is partially Dow's reading. Should be cited extensively in §1.4 line 68 area.

### Chunk 161 (pp.~197-198) — dist 0.3675, query: doxa-belief-emotion

> "Some such strategy is helpful to see off a worry that Aristotle had omitted here to include in his definition anything approaching the obvious requirement that a pathos be a mental state — something affecting the soul! [...] [The puzzle about epithumia seems to me to be softened by 1378a3 and especially 1388b32, which make it hard to deny that at least some kinds of epithumia count as emotions for Aristotle.]"

**Relevance**: Dow on the place of *epithymia* in Aristotle's emotion-taxonomy — directly relevant to the dissertation's coined term *epithymia* (replacing `pathos simpliciter`). Dow notes that at *Rhet.* 1378a3 and 1388b32, some forms of *epithymia* count as full *pathē*. Useful for the footnote-at-first-use of *epithymia* (per terminology-decisions-final.md §3.1).

### Chunk 192 (pp.~233-234) — dist 0.4055, query: doxa-belief-emotion (sun-example)

> "[The sun-example argument:] I have simply looked at the sun, seen it looking the way it normally looks, but have not changed in my belief about its size. In fact, there has been neither a change in the facts, nor anything that has escaped my notice. On that basis, as a result of seeing the sun, my belief about it has not become false in any way. This natural picture is [...] at odds with a view of phantasia as being a mixture, or weaving-together of belief and perception. Indeed, it cannot involve belief."

**Relevance**: Dow's reading of the sun-example argument — phantasia is NOT a mixture of belief and perception. This is the canonical 21st-century treatment of the *DA* III.3 phantasia-vs-doxa distinction. LOAD-BEARING for §1.3 (A3 modal-architectural framework) and §1.4 (doxa-as-cognitive-gate).

### Chunk 207 (pp.~250-251) — dist 0.4062, query: doxa-belief-emotion

> "Aristotelian passions simply do not seem to fit this pattern. For example, what 'appears' to someone experiencing praotês is a person towards whom they are feeling calm (this much is certainly such as could be perceived by the senses), appearing as not having done anything to insult them, or as having done those things [...]" + fn 297: "'It [viz. a change coming about by the exercise of perception, which will turn out to be phantasia] is bound to be similar to perception'. [DA 428b14] [...] phantasia involves representation of things as they would be perceived by the senses [...] 'States-of-appearance are just like states-of-perception except without matter.' [DA 432a9f]"

**Relevance**: Dow's structural account of phantasia-content as sense-perceptual but content-independent of matter. Bridges Aristotle's *DA* with the dissertation's three-grades-of-phantasia thesis from Papachristou.

### Chunk 172 (pp.~210-212) — dist 0.4085, query: emotions-as-pleasures-pains

> "First, it may be that Aristotle's view is that emotions involve mere appearances (how things look), where it is not part of the emotion that assent is given to these appearances. The emotion itself does not involve taking things to be a certain way, it involves their looking a certain way. A second option is that emotions do involve taking things to be a certain way, but the use of phantasia signals that this consists in (or results from) an unreflective assent rather than the kind of reflective assent that only humans can undertake. A third kind of position that Sihvola considers is that Aristotle's phantasia language sets out the minimum conditions for having an emotion: thus emotions need only involve appearances [...]"

**Relevance**: Dow's taxonomy of three readings of phantasia-emotion-elicitation (mere-appearance / unreflective-assent / minimum-condition). Useful for §1.4 Feedback Loop subsection discussion of how *resonant pathē* relate to phantasmata.

### Chunk 27 (pp.~37-39) — dist 0.3931, query: epithymia-orexis-pathē

> "[On Aristotle's normative constraints on rhetoric:] there are normative constraints on what will count as an exercise of this expertise and what will not. [...] Indeed, just such a point is part of what Gorgias appears to contend in Plato's Gorgias 456c6-457c3."

**Relevance**: Useful for §1.4 conclusion / §1.5 rhetorical-action material on emotion-arousal as legitimate technique.

Form the core of Dow's doxa-is-necessary-for-emotion argument. These three chunks together can serve as the dissertation's anchor for §1.4 doxa-as-cognitive-gate.

### Chunk 119 (pp.~147-148) — dist 0.4079, query: doxa-belief-emotion

Whether taken as a claim about the pathē themselves, or about their arousal, it just seems absurd to think that they cannot be about (say) the central issue of a trial."

**Relevance**: Dow's defense of the cognitive-content-of-pathē thesis. Useful for §1.4 articulationally-concrete *pathē* discussion.

### Chunk 56 (pp.~73-74) — dist 0.3979, query: rhetoric-ii-catalog

> "[On Aristotle's hypothetical-imperative reading of 'one should not warp the juror':] Some purpose, shared by orator and lawmakers, might relate to a basic concern for the proper functioning of courts. One such purpose that would be frustrated by warping the juror is avoiding distorted (or improperly formed) judgements."

**Relevance**: Bridges Aristotle's Rhetoric I.1 normative-constraints reading with emotion-arousal in II.2-11.

### Chunk 148 (pp.~181-183) — dist 0.4131, query: rhetoric-ii-catalog

> "It asserts categorically that these things are off-subject, and hence cites a preoccupation with these things as a reason to suppose that previous writers have failed to contribute anything (much) to the art of rhetoric. [...] How sympathetic one is to the restrictive reading of 'warp' (διαστρέφειν) at a24 seems to me to depend on one's view of the strength of the case built up elsewhere [...]"

**Downstream value**: Dow 2011 is HIGH PRIORITY for a future corpus/index pipeline — possibly the single highest-priority deep-analysis source given its 228 ingested chunks and direct LOAD-BEARING relevance for §1.4 doxa-as-cognitive-gate.
